name: Data Quality for AI
title: Data Quality for AI
answer: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. The work sits at the boundary between the warehouse and the model, and it treats the table as the unit of concern rather than the pipeline alone. A feature that is stale, duplicated or null in the wrong place will be learned as if it were true.

sections.body: Data quality for AI covers the accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness of the rows an AI system reads. Tests written in SQL, lineage records and data contracts are the usual controls, because a model cannot tell a wrong value from a right one. The work sits at the boundary between the warehouse and the model, and it treats the table as the unit of concern rather than the pipeline alone. A feature that is stale, duplicated or null in the wrong place will be learned as if it were true.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the same warehouses and lakehouses that hold the training and serving data, so SQL is the natural language for checks. Typical pieces are a scheduler that runs assertions on a cadence, a metadata store for lineage and column profiles, and a contract registry that records what each table promises to downstream consumers. Version control holds the test definitions, and alerting routes failures to the owning team. Some checks run at write time in the ingestion job, others run as scheduled queries against the landed table.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by profiling columns to learn their real ranges, null rates and cardinality, then write assertions that encode those expectations. Common tests cover uniqueness of keys, referential integrity between tables, accepted values in a categorical column, freshness of a timestamp, and row count within an expected band. Lineage is traced from source table to feature to model so a failure can be attributed. Contracts formalise the agreed schema and semantics, and a failing test blocks the downstream job rather than warning quietly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership matters more than tooling: every table needs a named team accountable for its contents and for responding when a test fails. Contracts turn informal expectations into reviewable commitments, and lineage gives auditors a path from a model output back to the rows that produced it. Access controls and audit logs record who changed a definition and when. Where personal data is involved, quality checks also support deletion and correction requests, since a stale or duplicated record can outlive the request that should have removed it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more checks to be generated from observed data rather than hand written, with anomaly detection proposing thresholds that a human confirms. Contracts are moving from documents into machine readable registries that pipelines enforce automatically. Feature stores and vector indexes are pulling quality concerns closer to serving time, where freshness and drift matter as much as correctness at rest. The open question is how much of this a model can police itself, and the working answer so far is very little.
